newsitem.title: FRANCE: Mideast violence scares world, Netanyahu blamed.
newsitem.headline: Mideast violence scares world, Netanyahu blamed.

text.p: World governments voiced alarm at an explosion of Israeli-Palestinian violence on Thursday and most, well beyond the Arab world, blamed hardline Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu for provoking a second Intifada.
The United States, Russia, France and Britain all appealed for calm and urged Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat to return quickly to peace negotiations.
Arab states hailed what they called "the Intifada of the Palestinian people" and said a tunnel Israel had opened in Arab East Jerusalem was part of a plot to destroy a Moslem shrine.

After at least 55 people were killed in riots and gun battles in the occupied West Bank and Gaza, U.S. President Bill Clinton said he has asked both Israel and the Palestinians to "end this violence" and resume peace talks.

Without openly apportioning blame for the worst bloodshed since the 1993 Israel-PLO peace accords, Clinton urged both sides "to avoid unnecessarily provocative actions", an apparent veiled reference to the Israeli tunnel under Jerusalem.
The United States is Israel's closest ally and the dominant power in the Middle East. A further blow-up could weigh on Clinton's campaign for re-election in November.
European and Arab nations pinned the blame squarely on the Jewish state's hawkish 100-day-old government.

By late Thursday, 44 Arabs and 11 Israelis had been killed in two days of widespread mayhem. Israel declared a state of emergency in the West Bank and Gaza Strip and sent in tanks and helicopters to quell the unrest.
Television images of the bloodshed recalled the worst days of the 1987-93 Intifada (uprising), in which Palestinians rose up against Israeli occupation.

At the United Nations, where the Security Council was due to discuss the crisis, the European Union and Islamic nations criticised Israel and urged it to prove its commitment to the crumbling Middle East peace process.

The Paris-based U.N. cultural agency UNESCO accused Israel of violating international principles by excavating in occupied land and, echoing Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak, urged it to close the tunnel.

Russia, co-sponsor with Washington of the Middle East peace process, said: "The fact that the Israeli authorities, in a unilateral fashion, opened a tunnel next to a Moslem holy site provoked a spontaneous protest by the Palestinian population."

France said the violent reaction was predictable. President Jacques Chirac, who urged Netanyahu in Paris on Wednesday to avoid provocations and return to land-for-peace negotiations launched by his Labour predecessors, telephoned Arafat to express his "solidarity and support" for the Palestinians.

Britain, Italy and Germany also faulted Israel. The violence wrecked Netanyahu's quest for European support, and forced him to cut short a three-country tour of Britain, France and Germany and rush home to handle the crisis.

Diplomats said there was concern in Western capitals that Arafat might not be able to control the explosion of Palestinian anger after months of perceived procrastination and humiliation by Israel and that it might trigger wider violence, possibly drawing in Lebanon and Syria.

"Many governments think Netanyahu is getting what he deserves for reducing the peace process to a crawl, going back on the agreement to withdraw from Hebron and resuming Israeli settlement in the West Bank. But the implications are frightening," said one European Middle East-watcher.

Norwegian Foreign Minister Bjoern Tore Godal, whose country brokered the 1993 Israel-PLO peace accords, told Reuters: "The broad unrest is a signal of the deep frustration among many sectors of the Palestinian community as a result of the lack of progress in the peace process.
"The tunnel and many other items are not large themselves but add together to heighten frustrations and lead to the sort of broad unrest we are seeing now."
